text: Everything gathered so far in this chapter, the requirements brief, the provider choice, the sizing numbers, comes together on paper before any of it comes together in a console. A rough sketch forces you to work through how the pieces actually connect before you've committed real resources, real money, and real time to building it.

A real architecture diagram answers three things clearly enough that someone else could follow it. Network layout: what subnets exist, and what's public-facing versus isolated. Compute tiers: what actually runs where, a web tier, a database tier, maybe a background job tier, each its own box instead of one blob labeled the app. And data flow: how a request actually moves through the system, from the user through each tier to storage and back.

Data flow is the piece most often skipped, and the one most likely to expose a real problem. Sketch it and you might discover the background job tier was assumed to reach the database directly, when it actually has to go through the application tier first. Caught on paper, that's a conversation. Caught after deployment, that's a rebuild of live infrastructure.

Every mistake a diagram catches is a mistake that never gets built. Realizing on paper that a database tier was about to sit on a public subnet costs nothing but a correction. The same mistake found after deployment can mean tearing down and rebuilding infrastructure that already has real user data in it, during a maintenance window nobody budgeted for. The diagram's whole job is moving that discovery to the cheapest possible moment.

A diagram drawn only to plan and then thrown away wastes half its value. Kept and updated as the environment changes, it becomes the first page of real documentation — what a new engineer looks at to understand what's actually running, and exactly what this course's documentation and handoff chapter builds on directly.

You now know what belongs in a real architecture diagram and why sketching it on paper saves real rework later. That closes out planning. Next, Chapter 2 starts the actual build, in the order a real deployment follows: the network layer first, before anything else goes in.
